text: Ludwig Georg Elias Moses Bieberbach (German: [ˈbiːbɐbax]; 4 December 1886 – 1 September 1982) was a German mathematician and a leading figure in National Socialist German mathematics ("Deutsche Mathematik"). Born in Goddelau, near Darmstadt, he studied at Heidelberg and under Felix Klein at Göttingen, earning his doctorate in 1910 with a dissertation titled On the theory of automorphic functions (German: Theorie der automorphen Funktionen). He began working as a Privatdozent at Königsberg in 1910 and became Professor ordinarius at the University of Basel in 1913. He taught at the University of Frankfurt in 1915 and at the University of Berlin from 1921 to 1945. Bieberbach wrote a habilitation thesis in 1911 on groups of Euclidean motions, identifying conditions under which the group must have a translational subgroup whose vectors span the Euclidean space—a contribution that helped solve Hilbert's 18th problem. He conducted research in complex analysis and its applications, and is known for work in dynamics in several complex variables, where he obtained results similar to Fatou's. In 1916, he formulated the Bieberbach conjecture, stating a necessary condition for a holomorphic function to map the open unit disc injectively into the complex plane in terms of its Taylor series. In 1984, Louis de Branges proved the conjecture, leading to the conjecture being sometimes referred to as de Branges' theorem. There is also a Bieberbach theorem on space groups. In 1928, Bieberbach co-authored a book with Issai Schur titled Über die Minkowskische Reduktiontheorie der positiven quadratischen Formen. He spoke at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Zurich in 1932. Bieberbach joined the Sturmabteilung in 1933 and the NSDAP in 1937. He actively participated in dismissing Jewish colleagues, including Edmund Landau and his former coauthor Issai Schur, from their academic positions and facilitated Gestapo arrests of colleagues such as Juliusz Schauder. He was heavily influenced by Theodore Vahlen, another German mathematician and anti-Semite, who, along with Bieberbach, founded the "Deutsche Mathematik" movement and journal. The movement promoted a "German" (in this case, intuitionistic) style in mathematics, with Bieberbach claiming that "the Cauchy–Goursat theorem arouses intolerable displeasure" in Germans, as it represented an abstract style of reasoning and "pronounced shrewdness" characteristic of "Jewish mathematics." Bieberbach's and Vahlen's concept of German mathematics was part of a broader trend in Nazi Germany to imbue the sciences with racial characteristics, including pseudoscientific movements such as "Deutsche Physik," "German chemistry," and "German biology." In 1945, Bieberbach was dismissed from all academic positions due to his support of Nazism, but in 1949 he was invited to lecture at the University of Basel by Ostrowski, who regarded his political views as irrelevant to his mathematical contributions.
